section_summary: This section follows Japan’s response to Soviet gasoline imports, the resulting price war, and proposals to place the oil trade under Japanese control. It documents the 1934 Oil Industry Law, American and British concerns about its licensing, storage, pricing, and sales provisions, and diplomatic discussions about protecting foreign companies. It also covers possible changes in Japan’s crude oil sources, including the Netherlands Indies and Rumania.

people.name: Kojiro Matsukata
people.role: Importer and distributor of Soviet gasoline in Japan

people.name: Kurusu
people.role: Director of the Commercial Bureau of the Japanese Foreign Office

people.name: J. C. Goold
people.role: General Manager of Socony-Vacuum Corporation in Japan

people.name: S. W. Washington
people.role: Third Secretary of the American Embassy

people.name: Malcolm
people.role: Representative of a foreign oil company

people.name: Kenzo Aoyama
people.role: Chairman of the Diet committee examining the Petroleum Industry Bill

people.role: Chief of the State Department’s Division of Far Eastern Affairs

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on Japan’s gasoline price war
subfiles.about: Reviews Tokyo despatch No. 522 and the prospect of greater Japanese government control of gasoline prices.
subfiles.summary: Japanese companies have cut prices to meet Soviet gasoline, risking losses and possible government intervention. An Embassy contact reports that greater control is likely.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 522: Japan’s Oil Problems
subfiles.about: Reports the impact of Matsukata’s Soviet gasoline sales and possible Japanese oil controls.
subfiles.summary: Matsukata’s low-priced Soviet gasoline has prompted Japanese firms to cut prices against the advice of foreign competitors. Grew considers whether the losses might encourage government intervention favoring Japanese producers. Kurusu of the Foreign Office says a licensing system and greater control are likely, while hinting that foreign companies should avoid new investment.

subfiles.title: Japan’s National Oil Policy
subfiles.from: Ballock A. Butts, Commercial Attaché, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Outlines competing Japanese proposals for a state oil monopoly or an import permit system.
subfiles.summary: The monopoly proposal would transfer oil rights to a semi-official company and absorb foreign assets. The alternative would license importers and manufacturers, favor crude oil through tariffs, and diversify crude supplies.

subfiles.title: Document file note for Despatch No. 541
subfiles.about: Cross-references a despatch concerning Matsukata and Japan’s unsettled oil policy.
subfiles.summary: Matsukata’s gasoline sales complicate the oil market; government policy remains undecided.

subfiles.title: Japan’s Oil Problem
subfiles.about: Summarizes the Soviet gasoline price war and signs of forthcoming Japanese oil controls.
subfiles.summary: Established companies cut prices to compete with Matsukata’s Soviet gasoline. The excerpt describes pressure on the firms, proposed national oil policies, and concern that government price setting could harm foreign companies.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on Despatch No. 562
subfiles.about: Reviews proposed consolidation of oil companies and a suggested American response.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum describes merger proposals that could remove foreign firms from active gasoline sales. It notes Navy objections and Socony-Vacuum’s suggestion of tying Japanese crude oil imports to gasoline purchases.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 562: Japan’s Oil Problems
subfiles.about: Examines the gasoline price war and a proposed merger under Japanese control.
subfiles.summary: Matsukata’s low prices have damaged established firms, although his own sales are declining. Japanese departments disagree over policy, but officials are considering a large company with Japanese control and possible foreign participation. Grew explains the difficulties of valuing foreign assets and the Navy’s fear of losing crude supplies. Socony-Vacuum proposes that the United States link crude oil exports to Japanese purchases of gasoline.

subfiles.title: Summary of Despatch No. 562
subfiles.about: Condenses Grew’s account of Matsukata’s sales and proposed consolidation.
subfiles.summary: Summarizes the price war, proposed oil company merger, and suggested American leverage over crude exports.

subfiles.title: Document file note for Despatch No. 580
subfiles.about: Cross-references a despatch on continued disruption from Soviet gasoline imports.
subfiles.summary: Matsukata declined to cooperate after being told of difficulties his imports caused.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on Despatch No. 624
subfiles.about: Notes Komatsu’s offer to help Socony-Vacuum with problems in Japan and Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Komatsu hopes to ease a Dairen kerosene dispute and concerns about discrimination against American goods.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 624: Conversation regarding oil in Japan and Manchuria
subfiles.about: Transmits a report of a conversation with Socony-Vacuum’s manager about Takashi Komatsu.
subfiles.summary: Grew forwards Goold’s account of Komatsu’s interest in easing Socony-Vacuum’s difficulties and improving Japanese-American relations.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation with J. C. Goold
subfiles.about: Records Goold’s account of Komatsu’s offer to help with oil disputes.
subfiles.summary: Komatsu discussed Dairen kerosene duties, a proposed Manchurian oil monopoly, and Soviet imports. He hoped to prevent a reputation for discrimination against American goods.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 39 from Tokyo on the oil control bill
subfiles.about: Reports an oil control bill and asks whether to make informal representations.
subfiles.summary: The bill would license refiners and importers, require stocks, and permit government price setting. Grew warns that its administration could force foreign companies out despite assurances from the Commerce Minister, and asks whether he should make representations similar to those of the British Ambassador.

subfiles.title: Department instruction to Tokyo on oil company treatment
subfiles.about: Authorizes informal representations seeking equal treatment for American oil firms.
subfiles.summary: Instructs Grew to ask Japan to accord American firms the same rights and consideration as Japanese firms.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on Despatch No. 701
subfiles.about: Reviews the proposed oil law and assurances given to foreign firms.
subfiles.summary: Notes that ministerial assurances may carry little weight and that the Embassy has been authorized to seek equal treatment.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 701: Bill for the Control of the Oil Industry in Japan
subfiles.about: Explains the proposed oil law, expected regulations, and concerns of foreign companies.
subfiles.summary: Grew details licensing, compulsory stocks and sales, price controls, inspections, and other powers in the bill. Foreign companies fear the law could gradually exclude them, despite a minister’s assurance that it aims to protect their business. He also reports press comment and opposition from motorbus and taxicab operators.

subfiles.title: Oil Bill Presented to Session of Diet
subfiles.about: Prints a translation of the proposed Japanese oil control bill.
subfiles.summary: The bill requires permits and oil stocks and grants broad supervisory, pricing, inspection, and penalty powers.

subfiles.title: Aide mémoire on foreign companies and the oil bill
subfiles.about: Records objections to an oil company merger and official assurances about the proposed law.
subfiles.summary: Foreign representatives explain that a merger would threaten their sales outlets, asset control, and secure markets. A Japanese official says the bill is intended to stabilize supply and promises equal protection for foreign and Japanese firms. The discussion also covers refinery permits, subsidies, tariffs, and the planned advisory committee.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 60 from Tokyo on passage of the Petroleum Control Law
subfiles.about: Reports passage of the law and possible expansion of crude imports from the Netherlands Indies.
subfiles.summary: The Diet has passed the law, but enforcement rules are pending. Grew explains his delay in making representations and warns that proposed barter arrangements could reduce American crude exports.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on representations to Japan
subfiles.about: Considers whether representations can protect American oil interests under the proposed controls.
subfiles.summary: The writer doubts that informal inquiries will clarify Japan’s policy, but urges a response showing concern for Socony-Vacuum and for American treaty rights.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on Despatch No. 734
subfiles.about: Summarizes Grew’s representations and the potential effect of Netherlands Indies oil purchases.
subfiles.summary: The memo notes fears that foreign firms may be excluded from future growth and that Dutch crude purchases may displace American oil.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 734: American Oil Interests in Japan
subfiles.about: Reports Grew’s request for equal treatment and assesses the new law’s effects.
subfiles.summary: Grew recounts his informal statement to the Vice Minister for Foreign Affairs, who promises to look into American concerns. He expects foreign firms to retain existing business for now but fears that growth will be reserved for Japanese companies. He also examines possible barter negotiations that could shift crude oil purchases from the United States to the Netherlands Indies.

subfiles.title: Oil Industry Law
subfiles.about: Provides the Embassy’s translation of Japan’s promulgated Oil Industry Law.
subfiles.summary: The law requires government permission for oil refining, importing, business plans, transfers, and mergers. It mandates oil stocks, permits compulsory government purchases and price orders, creates an advisory committee, and authorizes inspections, license cancellation, and fines. Supplementary rules cover existing businesses, oil in transit, and delayed enforcement of stock requirements.

subfiles.title: Document file note on promulgation of the oil control bill
subfiles.about: Cross-references a report describing the oil control law’s provisions.
subfiles.summary: Notes promulgation of the oil control bill and a summary of its provisions.

subfiles.title: Report excerpt on oil controls and Dutch East Indies barter
subfiles.about: Summarizes the new oil controls and a proposal to barter for Dutch East Indies crude.
subfiles.summary: The excerpt lists licensing, stock, sales, and pricing provisions. It also reports support for government crude purchases under a barter arrangement with the Dutch East Indies.

subfiles.title: Document file note for Despatch No. 664
subfiles.about: Cross-references a despatch outlining probable oil control bill provisions.
subfiles.summary: Points to Grew’s account of the expected Japanese oil control bill.

subfiles.title: Document file note on Rumanian oil and the gasoline war
subfiles.about: Cross-references a report on barter with Rumania and the continuing gasoline price war.
subfiles.summary: Notes proposed Rumanian petroleum barter and an unsettled price dispute with Soviet oil interests.

subfiles.title: Report excerpt on Rumanian petroleum and the gasoline war
subfiles.about: Describes a Rumanian petroleum barter proposal and continued Soviet price competition.
subfiles.summary: A Rumanian diplomat reportedly proposed exchanging petroleum for Japanese goods. The gasoline price dispute remained unresolved after Soviet interests rejected a quota offered by American, British, and Japanese companies.

subfiles.title: Document file note for Commercial Attaché Report No. 160
subfiles.about: Cross-references a report outlining the Oil Control Law effective July 1.
subfiles.summary: Points to an outline of the law passed by the Diet and effective July 1, 1934.

subfiles.title: Telegram from Tokyo on forthcoming petroleum law report
subfiles.about: Announces a detailed report on the law and company discussions with the Department.
subfiles.summary: Grew says his report is en route and Standard-Vacuum’s manager is urging discussions in Washington.

subfiles.title: Department telegram acknowledging oil company discussions
subfiles.about: Reports recent discussions with the president of Standard Oil of New Jersey.
subfiles.summary: States that the company president discussed Japan’s petroleum situation with Department officers on August 22 and 23.

subfiles.title: Department telegram to Tokyo on possible joint action
subfiles.about: Describes consultations with oil companies and possible cooperation with Britain and the Netherlands.
subfiles.summary: Company representatives proposed joint representations over Japan’s petroleum regulations. The Department says it would consider cooperation if the British and Dutch governments wished to proceed. It relays British concern about the cost of required storage tanks and reports a message to London expressing sympathy with objections to the law.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 495 from London on British oil concerns
subfiles.about: Relays a British Foreign Office memorandum on Japan’s petroleum controls.
subfiles.summary: Britain fears that Shell may have to invest heavily in storage without a reliable return and asks for the American position. A Foreign Office official suggests coordinated company and government action and calls the matter urgent.

subfiles.title: Department instruction to London on petroleum controls
subfiles.about: Authorizes a response to British concerns about Japan’s petroleum law.
subfiles.summary: The Department says American firms view the law’s requirements as potentially intolerable and that it will consider British and Dutch proposals for joint or concurrent action.

subfiles.title: Department telegram requesting a report from London
subfiles.about: Requests an account of British communications and directs the Embassy to make no new approach.
subfiles.summary: Seeks a report on Foreign Office exchanges amid British and Dutch representations to Japan.

subfiles.title: Standard-Vacuum letter on discriminatory gasoline sales quotas
subfiles.from: Kersey F. Coe, Standard-Vacuum Oil Company
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Department of State
subfiles.about: Complains that Japan ordered a reduction in Standard-Vacuum’s proposed gasoline sales.
subfiles.summary: Coe says the required quota cuts Standard-Vacuum below its recent sales level while Japanese refiners receive increases. The company has instructed its Yokohama manager to reject the cut.
